Equatorial Guinea - Black Beach Hell

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
This is the remarkable story Daniel Jansen van Rensberg who was illegally held in the notorious Black Beach prison is equitorial guinea because of his business partner Angabe who had close connections with President Obiongs son. There was a business dispute between van Rensberg and Angabe. He was arrested and hauled before a judge who said at most this is a civil case and ordered his release. However Angabe and his thugs with political connections threw him back into prison. A year later his release was ordered but ont he way to the airport he was kidnapped again and chucked back into prison. This is his story of how he survived, of how embassy officials had to play hide and seek with the thugs to get him out of the country. He is now suing president Obiongs son for 25 million rand. He is suffering seer post traumatic stress disorder at this stage.

Press Release:


Exclusive: Black Beach Hell
His story has the makings of a Hollywood blockbuster. But for Daniel Janse van Rensburg, the reality of life in Equatorial Guinea’s notorious Black Beach prison was nothing less than a living hell. Daniel was kidnapped and held captive without charge for almost two years following a failed business deal. In an exclusive television interview, Daniel tells Carte Blanche of the horror of imprisonment and surviving rotten food, disease and gangsters, before finally paying a bribe to secure his freedom.


Script:



BLACK BEACH SCRIPT

A few kilometers from the sea at the wilderness in the western cape lies the quiet village of Hoekwil. The pace is slow, something welcomed by Daniel Janse van Rensburg and his wife. It's a stark contrast from the horrors he experienced in Equatorial Guinea, an oil rich country, in West Africa.

LINK: More than 400 days that’s how long Daniel Jansen van Rensberg languished in one of the world’s most notorious prisons. Black Beach in Equatorial Guinea.

Imprisonment was never on his mind when he travelled the African continent on business. Aviation was his specialty.

Daniel: My father was a pilot so I have always loved airplanes and so on. I've never really had an interest in flying myself.

In 2012 he began working on a contract with Gabriel Mba Bela, also known as Angabe, whom he met many years earlier when he was the mayor of Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.

Daniel said that since 1999 he had been involved in various aviation projects with Angabe

This time around Angabe wanted to start his own airline. Daniel spent two years setting this up.

But In late 2013, Angabe unexpectedly cancelled the aviation contract with Daniel and demanded that he return the 50% he had been paid in advance. Daniel refused saying he was not liable for the amount and because he was unable to do so.

Daniel: You know a lot of money was spent trying to get the right planes, flying back and forth to South Africa, to Europe, even to the east.
John: So almost immediately Angabe started getting hostile and his initial reaction was to pick up the phone and start speaking to his contacts?
Daniel: Yah, yah.

Angabe called in the rapid intervention police who arrested Daniel. He was charged with theft and fraud and taken before a judge, who immediately threw out the case.

Daniel: He called Angabe’s lawyer and told him that you know you wasting his time. They are abusing the law. They must stick to the contract and that was it and he said I can go.
John: And that was supposed to be the end of the matter?
Daniel: Yah
John: But sadly it didn’t turn out that way?
Daniel: That was when everything went bad, very very dark.

Daniel knew that he had to get out of the country fast. South African Embassy officials who were aware of his situation accompanied him to Malabo airport He even made it through passport control but the rapid intervention police were lying in wait.

Daniel: And as I was about on the stairs Angabe came rushing in and he went ballistic and when the consul came Angabe grabbed him and he told him you know he mustn’t interfere. The consul himself stood back and I said but you’ve got to do something, what they are doing is illegal so he said he cant do anything.

He was in effect kidnapped and taken to Black Beach prison. It’s notorious for the brutalization and neglect of prisoners. As he was led towards the prison gate, he was horrified by what confronted him.

Daniel: Everybody runs to the gate looking and screaming and shouting and I remember a lot of pushing and shoving and slapping.

Even as he was being roughed up. His thoughts were on his family.

Daniel: I was worried more about my family actually and I knew it was going to destroy Melanie.

Melanie: I was shocked. I almost fainted from shock. I have a walk-in cupboard and I climbed in there and I just asked the Lord what is going on.

Local journalist Fran Kirsten who lives a few kilometers away from the Janse van Rensburgs home in Hoekwil covered the story and also provided support for the family.

Fran: Something just clicked within me and I think it’s the mother in all of the women, the nurturing, that I needed to look out for a girl who was on her own without her husband. She had met him at school so she had never been without him.

Abigail (Daniels daughter): At that stage I didn’t know if my dad would come back or if things would be okay. At that stage I just knew that whatever I do I have to stay strong for my mother.

There are incidents that Daniel still wont talk about but he told us of the beatings he witnessed, the rotten food, the overcrowding and how he almost died of malaria and typhoid as there was no medical care.

Daniel: You know there are so many diseases inside there and the dirt. There is no other way. You can’t wash yourself properly. You cant live hygienically.

But what disturbed him most was that men, women and children were all imprisoned together.

Daniel: How can you do something like…. how can you put a 12, 13 year old kid in here you know because they get abused and...

LINK: Then after 3 months Daniel was taken out of prison and taken before another judge who tried to broker a deal between him and Angabe. He was told that all he needed to do to secure his release was hand over a million rand.

Back at home the family was only able to raise R70 000. He was slung back into prison where he would spend a further 14 months. He kept sane by holding onto his faith, helping weaker prisoners, keeping fit and smuggling letters to his family.

LINK. Then a ray of light. A Spanish prisoner whom Daniel had befriended was released and made good on a promise to try and help him. He sent an attorney to see Daniel but unfortunately he came bearing bad news.

Daniel: He said he couldn’t find anything against me. There are no charges against me; there is no documentation of me being in jail.

The attorney said a R200 000 bribe to be paid to officials would be the only way to secure his freedom. He was given just one hour to achieve this. He managed to get a call through to his wife.

Daniel: When I phoned her I said, “Skarrabols don’t cry. Don’t get emotional. Just listen, do you, can you get any money?”

It was the first time that Melanie had heard his voice in 6 months.

Melanie: When I heard his voice I thought it was like a dream. I said Wow and he said I must get the money together and we must just believe. So luckily I was able to get the money.

Daniel walked out of black beach. 3 weeks later and again accompanied by embassy officials, he entered into Malabo airport. To his horror he saw Angabe’s henchmen circling.

Daniel: I was thinking jeez no god please not again. So I told the guy in Afrikaans listen we walking past the door, I’m going for the car.

He and an embassy official sprinted to a staff car and sped towards the safety of the South African embassy.

Daniel: I immediately got a call from a friend and he said as well, don’t leave the embassy they are going to kill you.

He contacted journalist Fran Kirsten back in South Africa asking her to alert the media of his plight.

Daniel: We just said please Fran let the dogs go, just run, and just go crazy.
Fran: And I must say the media were amazing. The entire national news sprung in, Sky news was there, everybody.

As a result the mood changed and the Equatorial Guinea government gave free passage for Daniel, to leave the country safely. . After a brief stop in Addis Ababa and JHB he finally touched down at George Airport in September last year to a rapturous welcome from his overjoyed family… Daniel was on home soil and safe at last.

Chris Schoeman: He went through absolute hell in that jail and he was not afforded any trial or any charge was ever put to him.

Advocate Chris Schoeman is outraged. He says the family had been promised that president Jacob Zuma would discuss Daniel’s illegal imprisonment with the president of Equatorial Guinea when he visited that country in 2014.

Chris: after his return, the department of foreign affairs in South Africa could not give any explanation of what had transpired at this so called meeting.

In mid February, Daniel launched proceedings in the Western Cape High Court against, Teodorin Obiang, the son of the president of Equatorial Guinea, who is currently the 2nd vice president. Daniel is seeking damages of 75 million Rand as he believes that Obiang, in his capacity as the political head of the armed forces, police and prisons ordered his incarceration and refused his requests for release on the instructions of Angabe. Daniel's lawyers have thus far managed to successfully obtain an interim order attaching two of Obiang's houses in Cape Town. At present Daniel can’t sleep, concentrate, is anxious most of the time and suffers bouts of anger, which appear to be symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress.

Dr. Panieri-Peter: Part of what makes a trauma is the memory of the trauma, in other words, that you cant shut the memory off, it is a disorder of haunting.

Dr. Larissa Panieri-Peter was horrified to hear about Daniel’s experience and believes he would profit greatly from treatment.

Dr. Panieri-Peter: One can help people slowly increase their function, return them to a working environment, help them manage, their relationship. Sometimes you actually have to bring their families in, their wives in, their children in. Help other people know how to behave in relationship to this person so that they also are reconnected with other people.

Earlier this month, Melanie and Daniel travelled to Cape Town to celebrate his 50th birthday with their children. At this stage friends are supporting him financially as he ponders his future and tries to find a job. He says his greatest gift though is making up for lost time with his family.

Daniel: We have suffered greatly as a family so we have got to spend a lot of time just to get that healing again.

The pace is slow, something welcomed by Daniel Janse van Rensburg and his wife. It's a stark contrast from the horrors he experienced in Equatorial Guinea, an oil rich country, in West Africa. LINK: More than 400 days that’s how long Daniel Jansen van Rensberg languished in one of the world’s most notorious prisons. Black Beach in Equatorial Guinea. Imprisonment was never on his mind when he travelled the African continent on business. Aviation was his specialty. Daniel: My father was a pilot so I have always loved airplanes and so on. I've never really had an interest in flying myself. In 2012 he began working on a contract with Gabriel Mba Bela, also known as Angabe, whom he met many years earlier when he was the mayor of Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea. Daniel said that since 1999 he had been involved in various aviation projects with Angabe This time around Angabe wanted to start his own airline. Daniel spent two years setting this up. But In late 2013, Angabe unexpectedly cancelled the aviation contract with Daniel and demanded that he return the 50% he had been paid in advance. Daniel refused saying he was not liable for the amount and because he was unable to do so. Daniel: You know a lot of money was spent trying to get the right planes, flying back and forth to South Africa, to Europe, even to the east. John: So almost immediately Angabe started getting hostile and his initial reaction was to pick up the phone and start speaking to his contacts? Daniel: Yah, yah. Angabe called in the rapid intervention police who arrested Daniel. He was charged with theft and fraud and taken before a judge, who immediately threw out the case. Daniel: He called Angabe’s lawyer and told him that you know you wasting his time. They are abusing the law. They must stick to the contract and that was it and he said I can go. John: And that was supposed to be the end of the matter? Daniel: Yah John: But sadly it didn’t turn out that way? Daniel: That was when everything went bad, very very dark. Daniel knew that he had to get out of the country fast. South African Embassy officials who were aware of his situation accompanied him to Malabo airport He even made it through passport control but the rapid intervention police were lying in wait. Daniel: And as I was about on the stairs Angabe came rushing in and he went ballistic and when the consul came Angabe grabbed him and he told him you know he mustn’t interfere. The consul himself stood back and I said but you’ve got to do something, what they are doing is illegal so he said he cant do anything. He was in effect kidnapped and taken to Black Beach prison. It’s notorious for the brutalization and neglect of prisoners. As he was led towards the prison gate, he was horrified by what confronted him. Daniel: Everybody runs to the gate looking and screaming and shouting and I remember a lot of pushing and shoving and slapping. Even as he was being roughed up. His thoughts were on his family. Daniel: I was worried more about my family actually and I knew it was going to destroy Melanie. Melanie: I was shocked. I almost fainted from shock. I have a walk-in cupboard and I climbed in there and I just asked the Lord what is going on. Local journalist Fran Kirsten who lives a few kilometers away from the Janse van Rensburgs home in Hoekwil covered the story and also provided support for the family. Fran: Something just clicked within me and I think it’s the mother in all of the women, the nurturing, that I needed to look out for a girl who was on her own without her husband. She had met him at school so she had never been without him. Abigail (Daniels daughter): At that stage I didn’t know if my dad would come back or if things would be okay. At that stage I just knew that whatever I do I have to stay strong for my mother. There are incidents that Daniel still wont talk about but he told us of the beatings he witnessed, the rotten food, the overcrowding and how he almost died of malaria and typhoid as there was no medical care. Daniel: You know there are so many diseases inside there and the dirt. There is no other way. You can’t wash yourself properly. You cant live hygienically. But what disturbed him most was that men, women and children were all imprisoned together. Daniel: How can you do something like…. how can you put a 12, 13 year old kid in here you know because they get abused and... LINK: Then after 3 months Daniel was taken out of prison and taken before another judge who tried to broker a deal between him and Angabe. He was told that all he needed to do to secure his release was hand over a million rand. Back at home the family was only able to raise R70 000. He was slung back into prison where he would spend a further 14 months. He kept sane by holding onto his faith, helping weaker prisoners, keeping fit and smuggling letters to his family. LINK. Then a ray of light. A Spanish prisoner whom Daniel had befriended was released and made good on a promise to try and help him. He sent an attorney to see Daniel but unfortunately he came bearing bad news. Daniel: He said he couldn’t find anything against me. There are no charges against me; there is no documentation of me being in jail. The attorney said a R200 000 bribe to be paid to officials would be the only way to secure his freedom. He was given just one hour to achieve this. He managed to get a call through to his wife. Daniel: When I phoned her I said, “Skarrabols don’t cry. Don’t get emotional. Just listen, do you, can you get any money?” It was the first time that Melanie had heard his voice in 6 months. Melanie: When I heard his voice I thought it was like a dream. I said Wow and he said I must get the money together and we must just believe. So luckily I was able to get the money. Daniel walked out of black beach. 3 weeks later and again accompanied by embassy officials, he entered into Malabo airport. To his horror he saw Angabe’s henchmen circling. Daniel: I was thinking jeez no god please not again. So I told the guy in Afrikaans listen we walking past the door, I’m going for the car. He and an embassy official sprinted to a staff car and sped towards the safety of the South African embassy. Daniel: I immediately got a call from a friend and he said as well, don’t leave the embassy they are going to kill you. He contacted journalist Fran Kirsten back in South Africa asking her to alert the media of his plight. Daniel: We just said please Fran let the dogs go, just run, and just go crazy. Fran: And I must say the media were amazing. The entire national news sprung in, Sky news was there, everybody. As a result the mood changed and the Equatorial Guinea government gave free passage for Daniel, to leave the country safely. . After a brief stop in Addis Ababa and JHB he finally touched down at George Airport in September last year to a rapturous welcome from his overjoyed family… Daniel was on home soil and safe at last. Chris Schoeman: He went through absolute hell in that jail and he was not afforded any trial or any charge was ever put to him. Advocate Chris Schoeman is outraged. He says the family had been promised that president Jacob Zuma would discuss Daniel’s illegal imprisonment with the president of Equatorial Guinea when he visited that country in 2014. Chris: after his return, the department of foreign affairs in South Africa could not give any explanation of what had transpired at this so called meeting. In mid February, Daniel launched proceedings in the Western Cape High Court against, Teodorin Obiang, the son of the president of Equatorial Guinea, who is currently the 2nd vice president. Daniel is seeking damages of 75 million Rand as he believes that Obiang, in his capacity as the political head of the armed forces, police and prisons ordered his incarceration and refused his requests for release on the instructions of Angabe. Daniel's lawyers have thus far managed to successfully obtain an interim order attaching two of Obiang's houses in Cape Town. At present Daniel can’t sleep, concentrate, is anxious most of the time and suffers bouts of anger, which appear to be symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress. Dr. Panieri-Peter: Part of what makes a trauma is the memory of the trauma, in other words, that you cant shut the memory off, it is a disorder of haunting. Dr. Larissa Panieri-Peter was horrified to hear about Daniel’s experience and believes he would profit greatly from treatment. Dr. Panieri-Peter: One can help people slowly increase their function, return them to a working environment, help them manage, their relationship. Sometimes you actually have to bring their families in, their wives in, their children in. Help other people know how to behave in relationship to this person so that they also are reconnected with other people. Earlier this month, Melanie and Daniel travelled to Cape Town to celebrate his 50th birthday with their children. At this stage friends are supporting him financially as he ponders his future and tries to find a job. He says his greatest gift though is making up for lost time with his family. Daniel: We have suffered greatly as a family so we have got to spend a lot of time just to get that healing again.

metadata.Summary: This is the remarkable story Daniel Jansen van Rensberg who was illegally held in the notorious Black Beach prison is equitorial guinea because of his business partner Angabe who had close connections with President Obiongs son. There was a business dispute between van Rensberg and Angabe. He was arrested and hauled before a judge who said at most this is a civil case and ordered his release. However Angabe and his thugs with political connections threw him back into prison. A year later his release was ordered but ont he way to the airport he was kidnapped again and chucked back into prison. This is his story of how he survived, of how embassy officials had to play hide and seek with the thugs to get him out of the country. He is now suing president Obiongs son for 25 million rand. He is suffering seer post traumatic stress disorder at this stage.
